newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ICCO chief says futures market is no panacea.
newsitem.headline: ICCO chief says futures market is no panacea.

text.p: Increasing use of cocoa futures may give farmers more certainty over revenues but it will do nothing to stop prices fluctuating, International Cocoa Organization executive director Edouard Kouame said on Thursday.
"It is a mistake to look to futures markets as the new panacea for the problems of commodity markets," Kouame told the "Conference on Commodities - Africa on the World Market."
Liberalisation in producer countries had shifted the emphasis onto the use of tools such as price-risk management to stabilise producers' incomes.
But there was a difference between the concept of reducing uncertainty and that of reducing price volatility.
"They are not the same, nor does one lead to the other," he said in a keynote speech to open the one-day conference.
He said futures markets should form part of the mix of elements for a sound commodity policy within the framework of a liberalised global market.

But the dismantling of marketing boards or the drastic reduction of their functions in producing countries had created "a series of problems such as the detrioration of quality and increase in trade risks."

The magnitude of the problem had prompted the ICCO to hold meetings with the World Bank, the European Union and other bodies calling for increased liberalisation "in order to bring to their attention the dangers of reform performed too hastily."
He said the ICCO was preparing, in conjunction with the lending institutions, a project to counter some of the detrimental effects of reforms.

He briefly touched upon the issue of the EU proposal on five percent vegetable fat use in chocolate instead of cocoa butter. Kouame said the directive, if adopted, risked breaking the latest International Cocoa Agreement.

"In the absence of any reliable methods of verification to ensure compliance with the rules on vegetable fats, the implementation of the EU directive could not prevent fraud, nor prevent the consumer being materially misled. This would be contrary to the letter and the spirit of Article 33 of the International Cocoa Agreement, and this is a factual statement," he said.
